rationale: The review describes antimicrobial studies using cinnamon and clove oils, including combinations, and intestinal experiments that assess clove preparations. These results do not supply an evaluation of eating ground clove for Parkinson falls.

The review cites a laboratory report that extracts safranal from cumin seed and discusses anxiety-related models elsewhere for safranal. It does not connect toasted cumin and a clinical anxiety measurement.

An included study compares olive and canola oil in broiler feed and measures performance and immune outcomes. It supplies no evidence from cold-pressed canola consumed by people with Parkinson disease for pain.

The case-report review documents anxiety in 16 and tremor in 14 of the 89 cases with details on initial presentation or laboratory results. A separate table provides a typical caffeine-content estimate for dark chocolate. These datasets do not yield a dark chocolate anxiety estimate or address dried date fruit.
Tremor is named in a checklist without an item-level observation or comparison. Extract and dose labels conflict, and the study used healthy rats.
The convenience study abstract does not supply a comparative cramp severity estimate, the fruit processing or the controlled model. Hormone correlation concerns cramp onset.

Cinnamon powder in warm water, compared with empty capsules, had lower VAS pain ratings in all three intervention cycles. Study used a different population and source of pain, was unblinded, and has baseline-table anomalies.
Regional field and citation notes describe multiple ingredients or preparations. They report intended uses without measured severity or grade-specific oil attribution.
